In one sentence: an aircraft operating position that plans, manipulates, and monitors fixed-wing aircraft under licenses, operator training, and operating rules, completes preflight preparation, flight manipulation and monitoring, communication coordination, and recordkeeping according to regulations, and accepts continuing refresher training.

The tasks of airline pilots, copilots, and flight engineers fall into four categories: preflight preparation (studying weather, notices, and route data, formulating flight plans and fuel plans, completing weight and balance and takeoff performance calculations, inspecting the aircraft and systems according to checklists, and coordinating with dispatch and the cabin crew); flight manipulation and monitoring (manipulating the aircraft through taxi, takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, and landing, monitoring engine, hydraulic, electrical, and avionics systems, managing the autopilot and flight management system, and collaborating according to standard operating procedures and crew resource management); communication and coordination (maintaining communication with air traffic control and flying according to instructions, coordinating with dispatch, maintenance, and the cabin crew, and reporting and handling abnormal and emergency situations according to procedures); and recordkeeping and compliance (filling in flight logs and operations records, reporting defects and events, participating in refresher training and simulator assessment, and maintaining the validity of licenses, medical certificates, and type ratings).
U.S. 53-2011 identity, tasks, and common job titles; not a Chinese license threshold.

Work environment | 53% work indoors every day in environmentally controlled conditions, and 74% work every day in enclosed vehicles (cockpits) or operate enclosed equipment (O*NET 53-2011.00 respondent proportions).
Precision requirements | 84% consider being exact or accurate extremely important, and 16% consider it very important; deviations in flight parameters, fuel, and performance data directly affect safety.
Error consequences | 77% consider error consequences extremely serious, and 12% consider them serious; decisions affect the safety of the aircraft and the persons and cargo carried.
Communication and collaboration | 75% are in contact with others continually, 78% have face-to-face discussions every day, and 65% consider teamwork extremely important.
Time pressure | 72% face time pressure every day, and 17% at least once a week; operations are affected by flight schedules, weather, and flow control.
Decisions and responsibility | 65% make decisions every day, and 58% have a great deal of decision freedom; 63% bear very high responsibility for the health and safety of other workers.
Posture and equipment | 74% sit continually or almost continually, and 63% use their hands to operate controls continually or almost continually; 67% consider the work highly automated or (25%) moderately automated.
Schedule and work week | 73% have irregular schedules (varying with weather, demand, or contract periods), and 27% regular; 57% have a work week of fewer than 40 hours, 23% have a 40-hour week, and 20% have a week of more than 40 hours; this is only a work-week survey item and cannot be used to infer how many overnight or night-flying hours it includes.
Competition and conflict | 42% consider competition extremely intense, and 39% consider it very intense; 26% encounter conflict situations every day, and 47% need to deal with unpleasant or angry people at least once a week.

The boundaries come down to four things: who flies and commands the aircraft, who provides air traffic control, who performs aircraft maintenance and release, and who formulates operator operating standards. Pilots manipulate aircraft and are responsible for flight safety within the scope of their licenses and operator authorization, and the captain retains final command authority; air traffic control is the responsibility of controllers; aircraft maintenance is performed according to institutional and personnel authorization, and independent release must separately meet the corresponding qualifications and authorization; operating standards and safety management are the responsibility of the operator and the civil aviation authority; matters beyond license category, type rating, or the operations manual must be escalated according to procedure.

Fictional teaching model L, for paper-based data verification only: empty mass 300 kg at position 2.0 m; sample box A100 kg at position 3.0 m; sample box B50 kg at position 6.0 m. Total mass W is the sum of the masses, moment M is the sum of mass×position, and weighted position X=M/W. Exercise valid version v2 requires W≤500 kg and 2.4≤X≤3.0 m; the old v1 cap of 3.2 m has lapsed. Positions are relative to this exercise's fictional zero point, and the data are not parameters of any aircraft. Feedback one F1: move A from 3.0 m to 4.0 m, mass unchanged; record the version and recompute W/M/X. Feedback two F2: on top of F1 add a 50 kg sample box C at position 5.0 m; the original message lacks C's position, so first mark it as undecidable and request the supplement, then recompute after receiving 5.0 m. Both rounds keep using valid v2 and must not switch back to old v1.
All materials are this page's editorial creation and do not use real flights, internal manuals, or real limits.

Work one: list v1/v2, the valid version, parameters, units, and each item's source. Work two: compute W, M, and X row by row for initial, F1, and F2, first registering F2's missing position.
Work three: after receiving the position, record the judgment, the reason for the conflict, and the handover request, without drawing flight-operation conclusions.

First freeze valid v2 and the initial parameters; state formulas, units, and four-decimal display clearly, and judge with unrounded values. Independent recomputation answers: initial W=450 kg, M=300×2+100×3+50×6=1,200 kg·m, X=2.6667 m, both items conforming to v2. F1: W=450 kg, M=1,300 kg·m, X=2.8889 m, conforming to v2. After F2's position is received: W=500 kg, M=1,550 kg·m, X=3.1000 m; the mass equals the cap but the position exceeds 3.0 m, so it cannot be judged conforming. Old v1's 3.2 m cannot be used. These are teaching-model judgments only and are not aviation operational or release decisions.

paragraphs: Mainland China CCAR-61-R5: PPL requires reaching 17 years of age, junior high school or above, and a valid Class II or Class I medical certificate; CPL requires 18 years of age, senior high school or above, and a valid Class I medical certificate, normally holding a PPL first, with special pathways under §§61.91/61.93 for state-aircraft experience and foreign licenses; MPL requires 18 years of age, bachelor's degree or above, and a valid Class I medical certificate; ATPL requires 21 years of age, senior high school or above, and a valid Class I medical certificate, holding a CPL and instrument rating or an MPL first.
